phonemes.desc: Smooth breathing; short epsilon opens the name without aspiration.
Single rho, a liquid that rolls between the vowels.
Long omega [ɔː], the sustained note at the end — desire prolonged.

pronunciation.approximation: "eh-ROSS" — with the second syllable held longer than English allows; the o is deep and sustained.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: ἔραμαι (eramai), "to desire, love"; ἔρως is the noun of desire

kin.label: Beekes
kin.form: possibly Pre-Greek; no secure Indo-European etymology

pronunciation.note: Erōs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἔρως contains both stress (acute on the initial epsilon) and length (the long omega). The macron on the final ō preserves the long vowel, while the accent position is implied by the Greek original. The name is the full scholarly form of the force that moves the cosmos.

domains.title: Desire
domains.subtitle: Attraction, Union, Cosmic Motion
domains.lead: Erōs is not merely romance. He is the attraction that makes things move toward each other: fire upward, water downward, god toward mortal, atom toward atom. In the earliest Greek cosmogonies, Erōs is a primordial power; only later does he become the mischievous child of Aphrodite.

cards.name: The Bow
cards.desc: His weapon makes the limbs go slack and the mind unmade; no god or mortal is immune.

cards.name: Wings
cards.desc: Desire is swift and sudden; it arrives before reason can arrange a defense.

cards.name: The Heart Aflame
cards.desc: The fire of longing — physical, spiritual, cosmic.

cards.name: The Rose
cards.desc: Flower of Aphrodite and Erōs; beauty that wounds as it invites.

mythology.lead: Erōs stands at the beginning in Hesiod and at the margins in Homer. He is one of the oldest gods, yet his stories are few — because his power is everywhere.

myths.title: Fourth of the Primordials
myths.text: Hesiod places Erōs fourth in the procession of being: after Cháos, Gaia, and Tartarus, but before the children of Night. "He is the most beautiful among the immortal gods," Hesiod writes, "he makes the limbs go limp and overcomes the intelligence and prudent counsel in the breasts of all gods and men" (Theogony 120–122).

myths.title: First of All
myths.text: The pre-Socratic philosopher Parmenides made Erōs the first of all gods to come into being — not a child of Aphrodite but the primal force of attraction that organizes reality. In this philosophical reading, love is not an emotion; it is a cosmological principle.

myths.title: The Cosmic Egg
myths.text: In Aristophanes' Birds (414 BCE), a parody of Orphic cosmogony, Erōs is born from an egg laid by Night. He then mates with Chaos in the womb of Erebus to produce the race of birds. The image preserves the older idea of Erōs as a self-generating power of union.

myths.title: The Roman Eros
myths.text: In Apuleius' Latin novel The Golden Ass, Erōs becomes Cupid, the lover of Psyche ("Soul"). The tale — of forbidden love, betrayal, and divine reconciliation — became the template for countless later stories, though it belongs to Roman, not archaic Greek, tradition.

lore.syncretism: The Roman Cupido inherited Erōs's arrows and wings but gradually shrank from a handsome youth into a plump, blindfolded infant — the Renaissance putto. In Plato's Symposium, Erōs is redefined as the longing for beauty and the ladder from physical desire to the Form of the Good. For the Stoics, Erōs was a natural affinity (oikeiōsis) that binds the cosmos. Freud divided the psyche into Eros and Thanatos, life-drive and death-drive, making the Greek god the name of everything in us that seeks connection, pleasure, and life.
lore.culturalLegacy: Erōs is one of the most productive words in European languages: "erotic," "erogenous," "erosion" (via the wearing-away of desire). He appears on Valentine's cards, in pop songs, in perfume advertisements, and in psychoanalytic theory. The image of the winged child with a bow — Cupid — is one of the most recognizable figures in Western art. Yet the archaic Erōs was more formidable: a beautiful young man who could unmake kings and gods. To restore the name Erōs with its long omega is to remember that desire is not trivial; it is one of the forces that turns the world.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Erōs is the least visible of the great powers because we experience him from inside. He is not a storm you watch from a window; he is the weather inside the room. Every longing — for a person, for a place, for a version of yourself — is a local manifestation of the same force Hesiod placed at the foundation of the cosmos.

The modern world speaks of desire mostly as consumer appetite or romantic plot. But the Greek Erōs is larger: he is the pull that holds atoms together and tears empires apart. To name him correctly is to admit that attraction is not an interruption of reason but one of its oldest engines. The heart has its own logic, and Erōs wrote it.
